blurb: The running goldenrod: upright stems topped with dense golden plumes that feed late-season butterflies and bees when little else is open. CSU's own note is the important one — it spreads by underground rhizomes, so give it room or a boundary.
water: Low to moderate; occasional deep soak in summer heat
spread: Spreads by underground rhizomes into broad colonies; needs room or containment
seasons: Dense golden plumes late summer into fall; upright stems die back in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 7,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun to part shade, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Clay or loam soils, per CSU — this is not a plant that needs sharp drainage, and it will take ordinary Front Range garden ground happily. Almost too happily.[1]
care.water: Low to moderate. CSU rates its moisture requirement low to moderate, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of spreading. Upright stems with spikes of flowers that attract butterflies and bees — and CSU notes plainly that it spreads by underground rhizomes.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from midsummer through to frost; CSU records the colour as yellow and the height as 12–36 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Read CSU's comment before you plant it: it **spreads by underground rhizomes**. In a mixed border it will outrun its neighbours; in a dry meadow, a bank or a hell strip it is an asset. Give it a hard edge, a mowed margin or a root barrier, divide it hard every couple of years, and cut it down in late winter. This guide's other goldenrod, showy goldenrod (*S. speciosa*), is the clumping, well-behaved alternative if you want the look without the running.[1]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: No documented culinary use in the authorities consulted. Worth stating: goldenrod does NOT cause hay fever.[1]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for Canada goldenrod, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it, and note that a folk record of goldenrod tea is not an authority-backed preparation. One myth worth killing, though, and CSU says it outright: goldenrod is **mistakenly blamed as a cause of hay fever**. Its pollen is heavy and insect-carried, not wind-borne; the culprit blooming at the same time is ragweed. Anyone with an Asteraceae allergy should still handle it accordingly.[1]
